subsections.subsection_title: FIRST QUESTION: SHOULD YOU PERFORM A DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION?

blocks.text: This is an important OSCE safety point.

If a woman has antepartum vaginal bleeding, especially where placenta praevia has not been excluded, do not proceed with a digital vaginal examination simply because the station says “examine the patient.”
“I would first establish the cause of the bleeding and exclude placenta praevia, usually with appropriate ultrasound assessment, before performing a digital vaginal examination.”
This is a classic examiner trap.

subsections.subsection_title: WHEN NOT TO PERFORM A VAGINAL EXAMINATION

blocks.text: Especially before placenta praevia has been excluded.
Follow the appropriate emergency protocol rather than mechanically proceeding with the examination.

content_groups.group_title: Q: Why do you offer a chaperone?

blocks.text: Because this is an intimate examination. A chaperone protects the patient's dignity and provides support and professional safeguarding.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What are the components of the Bishop score?

blocks.text: The presenting part is level with the maternal ischial spines.
The presenting part is approximately 2 cm below the ischial spines.
The presenting part is approximately 2 cm above the ischial spines.
Oedematous swelling of the fetal scalp resulting from pressure during labour.
Overlapping of fetal skull bones during labour.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What might severe moulding suggest?

blocks.text: It may suggest difficulty with descent and possible cephalopelvic disproportion or obstructed labour, particularly when associated with other signs.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What is the difference between effacement and dilatation?

blocks.text: Effacement is shortening/thinning of the cervix.
Dilatation is opening of the cervical os, measured in centimetres.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What is a favourable cervix?

blocks.text: A cervix that has characteristics associated with a greater likelihood of successful induction, assessed using parameters such as the Bishop score.
Never assume consent because the examiner told you to perform the examination.
Tell the patient what you are going to do before doing it.
